request.system:
You assist an automated astronomer who infers how a body moves from angles-only sky observations (ecliptic longitude/latitude seen from an observer whose orbit is known). Jan, the fitting engine, fits candidate model families by least squares and compares them by Bayesian evidence. You see numerical summaries of the current best fit and its residuals, and you propose the next candidates to fit.

A candidate is either a registered family (by exact name) or a new central force law: the radial acceleration f(r) in AU/day^2 (negative = attractive) as an expression in r (heliocentric distance, AU), GM (the Sun's, 2.959e-4 AU^3/day^2, fixed) and parameters you declare with bounds and an initial value. Allowed in expressions: numbers, + - * / **, parentheses, exp, log, sqrt, tanh, pi, r, GM and your parameter names (lowercase, letters/digits/underscore). Prefer the simplest law that explains the residual structure; a new parameter must buy a clear improvement. Reply "stop": true when the residuals are consistent with noise or further candidates are unlikely to help.

parsed.analysis: The fit is very poor: residual RMS is about 80 deg (288,200 arcsec), and the fitted noise sigma of 45 deg is implausibly large. Mean east residuals swing by up to about ±80 deg between time bins, which points to a mismodelled mean motion or apsidal precession rather than random noise. The two half-ellipse fits give very different periods (2775 vs 601 days) and about -30 deg/orbit of apsidal motion. That much precession is not what a pure inverse-square law produces. The free power law with n≈1.86 beats Newton by about 35 in ln-evidence, so the force falls off more slowly than 1/r^2 at r≈3.5–3.9 AU. Small perturbative additions (inverse-cube, Yukawa, linear) gave little gain. That suggests an additional slowly-varying attractive component, such as 1/r (flat-rotation-like) or a constant pull, rather than a tiny correction. Three candidates test this: Newton plus a 1/r term, Newton plus a constant acceleration, and Newton plus a free power-law component. These may also help the optimiser escape what could be a poor local minimum.

proposals.rationale: A 1/r term (logarithmic potential, like a flat rotation curve) makes the force fall off more slowly than inverse-square. This is consistent with n<2 in the power-law fit and produces apsidal precession. It adds only one parameter on top of Newton.
A uniform extra central pull is the simplest alternative way to flatten the effective force index and generate precession over the narrow 3.5–3.9 AU range.
A general extra power-law component on top of Newton. This lets the data choose the exponent of the extra force, and it nests the two one-parameter candidates above.
